newsitem.title: USA: Tech IPOs look rosier, summer volume light.
newsitem.headline: Tech IPOs look rosier, summer volume light.

text.p: Technology stocks grabbed centre stage in the sleepy summer initial public offering market after the sizzling debut of Internet access provider At Home Corp.
At Home more than doubled at its opening Friday, closing with first day gains of 62 percent, up 6-1/2 to 17.
At Home's service is 300 times faster than regular dial-up modems by linking customers to the Internet using their cable television coaxial cables.

"It was obviously a hot deal. Once it went out into the market, clearly the momentum had a life all its own," said Scott Ryles, a managing director at Merrill Lynch and Co. Inc., a co-lead underwriter of the offering with Morgan Stanley Dean Witter.

The gains came even though the start-up has never posted a profit and may not for years, analysts said, showing investors are again willing to venture into unproven concept stocks, which bodes well for technology IPOs.

A surge in demand for techs and small-capitalisation companies added to the euphoric atmosphere. The Nasdaq Composite cracked the 1,500 level Friday, gaining 11.69 points to close at 1,502.62 in what has been a string of seven straight record closing highs.
But the exuberance for techs could prove short-lived as investors tire of waiting for the payoff.
Lary Aasheim, vice president at CoreStates Investment Advisors Inc. said he did not buy At Home stock because profitability was just "too far down the horizon" -- three to five years away.
"It is going to take a lot of money for some of the upgrades that have to happen for this company to take off. There are hurdles to them becoming profitable," said Aasheim.
At Home was lent credibility because it was a "showcase" IPO, set out before institutional investors for several years, he said. It also has strong ties to cable companies.
Aasheim said another tantalizing possibility that could have added to At Home's shine was whether it can someday win advertising revenues.

Merrill Lynch's Ryles added that the IPO was not as easy a sell as it might look at first blush, because of the start-up nature of the firm and because many fund managers were still smarting from losses in the sector earlier this year.

Technology IPOs on deck this summer that could benefit from the favourable mood include technology trade magazine publisher CMP Media Inc, sports Web site SportsLine and At Entertainment. With no tech deals in the works this week and light volume,

the theme is real estate. The hottest deals on deck look like CCA Prison Realty Trust, a Maryland real estate investment trust (REIT) that owns correctional and detention facilities, and LaSalle Partners, a Chicago manager of more than 300 U.S. properties.
REIT stock offerings have been popular as a defensive play on Wall Street lately, but the IPOs are generally known for raising a lot of money at once, not for one-day surges.

Another strong deal is a large stock offering by Switzerland's Sulzer Orthopedics Ltd., a maker of orthopedic and cardiovascular products. Morgan Stanley Dean Witter will lead the offering of 23.0 million American Depositary Shares to sell for roughly $21 to $24 a share.
About 10 companies are set to go public this week, according to a Reuters tally.

Mutual funds that invest in technology and smaller market caps outpaced their blue-chip counterparts last week with gains of 3.22 percent, according to Lipper Analytical Service. One notable blue chip IPO, Polo Ralph Lauren Corp., "broke issue" and fell below its $26-a-share IPO price last week.
